utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, Madam Registrar, and good morning, everybody. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are here. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Mitchell, Mr. Vanderpuye, Mr. Thayer. Defence I see absent Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Bourgon, and Mr. Josse, and Mr. Haynes from what I can see. So I understand you have something to tell us, Ms. Fauveau. Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, we mentioned the schedule during the Pre-Defence Conference, and we requested two additional days for recess, and my colleagues and myself are very grateful to you for having granted us those two extra days. However, we had a meeting between the Defence counsel, and we had discussions about various matters related to the trial and about the things we are supposed to do during the summer recess, and we came to the conclusion that it will be very difficult for us to complete all these tasks with just two weeks and two days of vacation. But summer recess does not mean that we are not going to perform any work. We are aware that the team that has completed the presentation of its case is waiting for a decision of the Appeals Chamber. All the other Defence teams are supposed to put their case yet, and all the teams -- most of the teams will spend most of their time during recess in the field, and all that time is not sufficient for us to complete all the tasks we are supposed to accomplish. Contrary to the Prosecutor, the Defence teams have only two counsel each. It's very risky to send one of us, one of the counsel in the field when the court is in session, because if one of us has a problem, then we would have to interrupt the trial. All the teams have investigators, but these investigators are not of the same calibre as the investigators of the OTP. Therefore, it's absolutely essential for us counsel to spend some time in the field. Because of all these difficulties, we would like to request three additional days for recess and to set the date for the beginning of the trial to the 25th of August. This is not the only problem we have to deal with. All of us have our own offices in our respective countries. We have things to do there. We have administrative and tax-related tasks to accomplish, and between the 1st and the 15th of August there is nothing we can do because it's a period where everybody's on holiday in our respective countries. Finally, let me say that up until now the trial had been going on in a very positive atmosphere with a good understanding between the parties. I believe that this good climate, this good understanding is partly due to the schedule we have had so far with regular breaks that allowed us to rest and to prepare the next hearings for them to run very smoothly. Obviously tensions are rising when people are tired, and I believe that at this very moment all of us are extremely tired. Without these three additional days I believe that we'll come back to the Tribunal just as tried as we are now at the end of August. This is a very long trial, but this is mostly a multi-accused trial with seven parties. It's a very complex trial. We are very aware of the deadlines set for this Tribunal, and we are convinced that we'll be able to fulfil and to comply with these deadlines, and we hope that we'll be able to complete the trial in the same spirit of cooperation and mutual respect as so far. For all these reasons, for all the reasons related to this trial and for what I would call human reasons, the Defence teams, in agreement with the OTP, are requesting three additional days for recess and are asking for the trial to begin again on the 25th of August. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Anybody else wishes to add anything to that? All right. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we will of course be prepared to proceed as directed, though this is my home leave here and I had already made plans to be away that week. So I won't be here that week, but my team, of course, will be ready to proceed, but -- so how that works into the mix, I just wanted to let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's for -- for you personally it's neither fish nor fowl, but for the rest of the team it could be. All right. We'll come back to you on this later on. Now, yesterday, Mr. McCloskey, towards the end of the sitting, you raised an issue having your concerns about the way Beara Defence team have been proceeding with their case when it relates to the information that is due to the Prosecution before the arrival or before the testimony of each witness. You would -- those of you who have understood me over the years would know exactly why I said -- I stopped the discussion there and then and I said we'll sleep over it, because it was indeed a matter of great concern. There is a lot involved, and Mr. Ostojic had left in the meantime. I was sure that given a little bit of time everyone would have thought about it, including ourselves. We, of course, discussed after the -- after your complaint we had a short discussion, and we each have thought about the matter in the interim, and we share your concerns. Let me use a very moderate phrase. We are very unhappy with the situation, pretty much like you are. So Mr. Ostojic will be back by Monday, as he said. In the meantime, given the importance of the matter that you have raised, and in our minds between yesterday and today it has increased in importance, I think the best way for you to go about it is to formalise it in writing if there is, on our part, to be a proper order like the one that you referred to that was handed down in the Stakic case. So you -- however, however, between now and when we hand down -- hand down the order, if that becomes necessary, we don't want you to be prejudiced, and therefore what we are telling you for the time being as an interim provision, for safeguard, is the following: that should during the testimony of the next witness -- witnesses, until this is finalised, there be matters that -- or issues that the witness are -- witnesses are asked questions about of which you have not had prior notice, in other words, if you're taken by surprise at any given moment, unless it is clear that a new issue has arisen in the wake of previous questions and could not have been anticipated, then we are reserving to the Prosecution the right to ask for a postponement of your cross-examination. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. At the time I spoke, I did not -- and I was responding to Mr. Nikolic, I was not fully aware of how the new news about that -- I think it's Mr. Pereula, affected Mr. Nicholls. I've spoken to him. He is ready to go and should be ready to go, though the next witness, Mr. Kerkez, this colonel from the Main Staff transport issue, there's no new issue on the table. The 65 ter report said he would talk about coming to Potocari and Bratunac on the 12th of July. The proofing note we received a day or two ago said he would be talking about coming there on the 12th of July. This morning when I got to my e-mails, I'm informed that there was a typo and that he is -- will be speaking of coming there on the 13th of July. Now, the difference between the 12th and the 13th when you're reviewing documents and intercepts and all the massive material to prepare is rather massive. I'm from the old school where I used to find out about Defence witnesses by looking behind me and seeing who came in the door, and I'm -- I can be ready for that. You will not get a good presentation from the Prosecution as you would have otherwise. So we will be ready for this witness despite this situation, and I hope I do not have to ask that a witness would come back. But the saga continues, and we are preparing the -- the response to this matter that has been dealt with somewhat by filings, and we'll get that to you very soon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Do you wish to comment, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I do feel the need to clarify certain matters. After the -- yesterday's day of work and your caution, in the course of the afternoon we made contacts through court officers, and I believe that our cooperation with the OTP is on the uphill, and I am sure that the absence of Mr. Ostojic will not affect the proceedings, as not done so far. I believe that everything that needs to be completed in time today and tomorrow will in fact be completed, and we have informed all the -- all those who need to know about that. I believe that the best way to proceed when it comes to the matters that need to be corrected in terms of what the witness will testify about can be done with the witness today in the course of his evidence. Let me use this opportunity to highlight the reasons that I mentioned yesterday when I said that we were not prepared for Spiro Pereula and his testimony, but I will state that we are prepared, nevertheless, to proceed with his testimony after Mr. Kerkez's evidence. Spiro Pereula will be speaking about the same matters that another witness we, Erdemovic has already testified about so the Prosecution is aware of that; although, I must say that we have not had the time to make note of the proofing session we had with him yesterday afternoon. If we so decide, I would like those who are in charge of that to make sure that Mr. Pereula is contacted and brought here to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When did he arrive here in The Hague? Mr. Nikolic, when did he arrive here in The Hague, Pereula?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He arrived in The Hague the day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps if one of Mr. Nikolic's associates could meet briefly with Mr. Nicholls now just verbally, that would be great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. I think -- I was thinking exactly of giving you five minutes to talk a little bit amongst yourself, Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Nicholls or Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have Kerkez first so that's the next witness. So there's -- if they can just see Mr. Nicholls at some point, we can get that established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you will meet during the first break, and in the meantime we can start with the first witness, Kerkez. We need -- okay. We need to process the documents relating to Debra Komar's testimony first, because we didn't do that yesterday. Mr. Nikolic, you have circulated a list of ten documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The list of documents admitted in the course of Mr. Ostojic's examination of yesterday was submitted. If necessary, I can read them all out, but I don't think there's any need for that. The list was filed after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections from any of the other Defence teams? None. Right. So they are all admitted. I don't know that they were all used with the witness, but I have my doubts in relation to one or two of them, but anyway. Mr. Vanderpuye, let's see first. Any of the other Defence teams? I wouldn't think so, have any documents? Mr. Sarapa? You cross-examined the previous witness. Do you have any documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No, there were no documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have a 65 ter 3551 which is the statement of Dean Manning dated 24th November 2003. In addition to that we have 65 ter 3479, which was the example -- I'm sorry. That's under seal. Which was the example of a match report that I used with Dr. Komar. I just wanted to mention in respect of this particular exhibit, during the examination of Dr. Komar, although she agreed with me that the number indicated on it was 29.5 trillion, in fact it is 29.5 billion, and I just wanted to make that clear for the record. The -- in addition to these two exhibits, Mr. President, in light of the events of yesterday, I think it is necessary to establish for the purposes of the record at least when these ICMP data disclosures occurred, and in particular the one related to Mr. Manning's 8 June 2007 exhumation report or summary. I have the disclosure dates of those documents in letters. They're not marked. Obviously we can assign them numbers with your permission, but I thought it was important that the Court be aware that that data was disclosed to the Defence on 6 July 2007, well in advance of obviously Dr. Komar's testimony. And I would also point out that her -- the annex to her -- to her report itself makes reference to two separate ICMP data spreadsheets in relation to these individuals, and we've had exactly two disclosures with respect to that except for the most recent one this July. So I thought that was important, and with your permission I would offer those as well into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections? Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections from any of the other Defence teams? None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dean Manning's statement was not admitted earlier, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't believe that one was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're tendering all of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is no opposition from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There's no opposition, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So these documents are all admitted. We can proceed with the next witness, Zeljko Kerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Kerkez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And as Presiding Judge, I welcome you to this Tribunal. You're going to testify in the Popovic et al. case. You've been summoned as a witness by the Defence team appearing for Colonel Beara. Before you start giving evidence our rules require that you make a solemn declaration to the effect that you will be testifying the truth, texts of which is going to be handed to you now. Please read it aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us. In other words it will be the equivalent to an oath to testify to the truth as it exists in many jurisdictions. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, a caution may be appropriate for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do you agree, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkez, I do not know what questions will be put to you in the course of your testimony, but it could well be that questions are put to you that if you answer truthfully could possibly expose you to investigations and possible criminal proceedings. In such cases, our law, our rules, provide a safeguard in favour of the witness. Our rules give you rights. But as I will be explaining to you, these are not absolute rights. Let me simplify it as much as I can. If such a question is put to you and you feel, rightly or wrongly, that it could expose you to criminal proceedings, if you consider such a question as an incriminatory one, in other words, then you can ask us for protection, the protection being asking us to exempt you from answering such a question. We will, of course, hear what you will have to say, and then using our discretion, we will decide whether to grant you such an exception or whether to order you to answer the question. If we grant you such an exception, of course we move to the next question. If we order you to answer such question, then provided your answer is truthful, anything you say, because you have been ordered by the Trial Chamber to say it, cannot be used against you in any proceedings that might be instituted. Have you understood what I have tried to explain to you in simple terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Nikolic will go first. He will then be followed by others on cross-examination. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kerkez.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before we start with your examination, let me make some preliminary remarks regarding the examination technique. We have to bear in mind the fact that our discussion has to be interpreted. This means that we have to leave enough time for the interpreters to accurately interpret what we're saying. We will achieve this by making a pause, both of us, before giving an answer or putting a question. Also, I would urge you to speak a bit more slowly. I hope you understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkez, we will formally introduce ourselves now. I'm Predrag Nikolic. I'm a member of the Defence team for Ljubisa Beara. Please introduce yourself. Give us your full name, date of birth, place of birth, father's name.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: My name is Zeljko Kerkez, a retired colonel. I was born on the 28th of December, 1951 in Kozarac, Prijedor municipality, Bosnia and Herzegovina. Father's name Lazo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is your educational background, Mr. Kerkez? What are your qualifications?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I completed the elementary school in Bac municipality in Vojvodina in Serbia. Technical high school -- the technical high school I graduated from in Novi Sad in 1970. I graduated from the technical military academy in 1977 in Zagreb. I have -- I am the -- with the rank of second lieutenant, and I also graduated from the technical military academy in the field of transport support with a -- and that's the master's degree I received from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe your career up until 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: After I graduated from the academy I -- in 1975 I started working in Titograd -- or, rather, in Podgorica in Montenegro in the military police training centre where I was platoon and company commander. I stayed there until 1978 when I went back to the technical academy as a teacher in the field of traffic where I received my master's degree and continued as a professor at the academy. After the start of the war in 1991, I was in Zagreb. I was in a sort of blockade there for some six months, and I had to evacuate my family because they were endangered. In 1992 when -- in 1991 when the agreement was reached, I withdrew with my unit to Belgrade, and up until 1992 I continued with my tenure as professor. I was the head of the department at the academy. And after the start of the war in Bosnia, I felt it my duty to volunteer to become a member of the army of Republika Srpska in order to protect the people there and to help form the army. I went to the army of Republika Srpska in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You said that you felt it your duty to report, to become a member of the army of Republika Srpska. Can you tell us why that was so?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: By birth I'm a Serb from Bosnia. I felt it my moral duty to protect the Serb people who were endangered at the time. For that reason, I reported to become a member of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What was your first duty and in which unit of the army of Republika Srpska? Just take it slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: My first duty as when I actually arrived there in January 1993. I went to Drvar, to the 2nd Krajina Corps, because this is the area that I was born in, if I can put it that way, and I became chief of the traffic and transportation service in the corps. I stayed there until September 1993 when I was transferred to the Main Staff in Han Pijesak. Also, as a chief of the department for traffic and transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So you arrived in the Main Staff practically to continue with your own line of work; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain your position, rather, in this organisational structure of the army? This traffic and transportation department, where did it belong in terms of establishment?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I was in the logistics sector that had several departments, including my own. The obligation of that department and my own and of my assistants was planning, organising, and carrying out all transports of materiel, technical resource and manpower and movement of personnel at army level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please be a bit clearer? Could you please tell us what does this mean, movement of units at the level of the army and of materiel and technical resources -- just a moment, please. Let me finish. For example, if from a particular area in Herzegovina some units have to be transported or some technical resources or materiel to another area, what is your task? What is the task of your service?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Planning of transportation at army level means the planning and realisation of all these movements among units at corps level. That is to say, if transport is supposed to take place from the Hercegovina Corps, say a unit was to be transferred to Krajina, that is to say, to the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps that had to go through my staff -- or, rather, through my department. So that is where the transport was planned, including fuel and all other material resources that were needed, or if a larger amount of materiel was supposed to be transported from the territory of one corps to the territory of another corps, that's the way that was done too, or if a logistics base was supposed to be supplied with a large amount of materiel from suppliers who could have been in the territory of the republic or outside the territory of the republic, again this went through my department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What does that mean that it went through your department? What form did your decision take, this planning of yours, I mean.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: If the order came from the logistics assistant or from a higher level, from the commander or the chief of staff, then I would do that straight away as ordered. If the request would come from the corps, I would receive a written request from the corps. Of course including elements as to what was needed, what quantity, and when. Then my department would make a plan and ensure transport, vehicles, fuel, the route that would be taken and so on. As for the time of execution --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How was your proposal then carried through?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I don't really understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You planned to use a certain amount of resources on the basis of a certain request, a certain number of buses or trucks, for instance. Who do you submit that to, and how will these resources be used?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Well, the plan is submitted to the requesting party and to the unit that is supposed to carry this through. Say if it's from the automobile battalion of the Main Staff, of course the plan -- the order, rather, should be sent to that unit in terms of who they should report to and what they should do at what time. And of course whoever requested that should know that their request had been granted and when it would be carried through.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to present a document to you, and then we're going to have a look at it and then you're going to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please display 2D550? We have a draft translation of the document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you see the text? If you cannot see it, then we can perhaps ask for it to be zoomed in. Thank you. Please take a look at this and read it slowly, and when you're ready, then we're going to discuss it. Can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is a document from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, from the logistics sector precisely. Could you explain this to us? What does this document mean from your point of view, from the point of view of the transportation service?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Sorry, I haven't seen the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please scroll down so that we see who signed this document. Please go ahead. Could you please explain the significance of this document to us? What is being asked for, and what are you proposing? Who does it come from? It says "Assistance in manpower, transport," et cetera. Could we please see the top part of the document so the witness can see what it was that I was talking about. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: This request is a response to the request of the Drina Corps when they asked that we provide them with a certain number of vehicles so that they could carry out appropriate transportation tasks. Well, we are telling them that we cannot meet their request because we have similar obligations. So they can carry out that task using their own resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: For the transcript, let us just note that the document is dated the 2nd of December, 1994. I'm going to go back to this now, what it says in this reply. "Carry out the mentioned tasks with your own resources." What does that mean? Does that mean that your logistics sector had resources of its own that it sent out to assist certain units?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The Main Staff had a unit that was -- that was intended for transporting units at battalion level, and they were used only for such purposes when interventions had to be carried out at army level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If I understand what you're saying, that means that the Main Staff had an opportunity to help in certain situations through this vehicle base of its own.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes, if there were needs of that kind and if there were requests coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to show you another document now. Could we see 2D549. Again we have a draft translation as well. Can you see it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you read it and then we'll see what this is all about. This is also a document of the Main Staff, the -- the sector for logistics. The 4th of June, 1994, is the date. Could you please tell us briefly what the content of this document is, what is being asked for, and what is the response of the logistics base?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: An order is issued here to the 63rd Automobile Battalion to carry out transportation. There are three tasks here. On the 8th of June is the first one, transport -- I mean, transport, well, in Milici -- I mean carry out appropriate transport for this Milici Brigade, and the second task is on the 12th of June that around 40 soldiers are to be transferred from Han Pijesak to Banja Luka and also the time when this is supposed to be carried out is specified. This is transportation between two corps, and that is why the Main Staff is issuing a task to -- issuing an order to have this task carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So how did you put this? If it has to do with transportation in territory of two or more corps, what is your role then?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The role is to carry out planning, to provide transportation resources, and to have this carry out in realtime. In a realistic time frame work, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In this document it says it was -- it was submitted to the 63rd Automobile Base --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Sorry, battalion. And cc'd to the Drina Corps. Is that what you were saying a few moments ago, that the Main Staff had resources of its own and from time to time provided assistance to others?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that such assistance could be rendered only on the basis of requests?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, was there a similar organisation of the transportation service at lower-level units, corps, brigade? Down to which level of unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The organisation of transportation -- of the transportation service at lower-level units, it was based on the same principle. That is to say at corps and at corps-level units, there was a transportation service with its own head and possibly another officer. This head was subordinated to his own assistant commander for logistics and to the commander and the chief of staff. Just like I was in a way. Also, there was the desk officer of the transportation service who also carried out this duty within this unit. Likewise, he was subordinated to his own assistant commander for logistics, to the commander, and to the chief of staff. Let me add one more thing. I could not issue orders to the chief of staff, for instance, to the chief of the transportation service in the corps. This was along professional lines only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You've just answered my next question. So the relationship you had with subordinate units -- or, rather, appropriate transportation services, it wasn't one based on hierarchy in terms of issuing orders.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So what did it consist of then? What was the substance of this relationship?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The substance was the one that I've already explained, assistance in planning and -- I mean, assistance along professional lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell us, please, passenger vehicles, official vehicles that were used by officers of the Main Staff, how and in which way was this question regulated, the use of these vehicles, rather?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: At the level of the Main Staff within headquarters there was the division for passenger vehicles. It was subordinated to the command of the staff administration. There was a commander there. And as for the professional aspect of it, I carried out those duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say planning?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: In terms of use, that is say that the officers on the Main Staff had certain needs, namely, to travel, to tour certain units, et cetera, so then they had to use vehicles. Of course they would submit requests. However, I have to point out that the commander, the chief, and the assistant commanders, they had their own vehicles assigned to them, and they had their own drivers who were with them all the time, whereas others were free, if I can put it that way, and were used upon request only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, only assistant commanders had vehicles and drivers that were assigned to them and that they could use at all times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before you answer the question. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you rephrase it, Mr. Nikolic, please. It is leading, undoubtedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Upon whose request were vehicles assigned for regular use?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Some of the senior officers, namely commander, chief of staff, and assistant commanders, had vehicles assigned to them on a permanent basis complete with drivers. They were free to use them at any time and at their own discretion. Let me stress the following: that the only exception in addition to these senior officers was the sector for security and intelligence where chiefs of departments of that particular sector also had vehicles. All the other vehicles were used by senior officers as needed for specific tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In what way was the right to one's own vehicle and driver regulated when it comes to these persons you've just indicated?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: This was regulated in the rules and in commanders' orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know which individuals in the security administration or, rather, in the sector for security and intelligence, also had vehicles assigned to them for daily use?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: In addition to General Tolimir, who was assistant commander, such a right was also enjoyed by the chief of the security department, Colonel Beara, and the chief of the intelligence department, Colonel Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The vehicles which were assigned to them for their regular use along with drivers, were records kept of them and where for possible review and control?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The records were kept in the relevant department, whereas the documentation was processed by my department or specifically by the desk officer of my department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In what way was the process of assigning drivers regulated? Was this process by your department or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: In -- except for the commander's driver who was chosen personally by the commander, the other drivers were selected by the traffic and transportation service upon request.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to recall the names of drivers that were used? Specifically, do you recall the name of Ljubisa Beara's driver?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I do not remember all of them, but I do remember most of them. I remember some of their names. Even today I happened to come across some of them. I recall Rajak who was General Milovanovic's driver. I recall Gvero's driver, Zoranovic. I remember Tomovic Milos was Ljubisa Beara driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, stop. Mr. McCloskey, I let him go because we were talking of names, and I figured out that your intervention --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could just be more -- a little specificity. It was long war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sure there were lots of drivers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you are more specific to either a particular period during the war or more than one particular period, please try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something I was just about to do, to clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In what period of time were you at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: As I said, from September 1993 through to the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify what you mean by the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Until the Dayton Accords -- or, rather, until 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In that period of time, that's to say between 1993 and 1997, as you say, did the previously mentioned individuals have drivers on a regular basis and always the same ones, or did they change?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: As a rule they always had the same drivers save for the situations where the drivers were absent, on sick leave, or where the individual concerned insisted that his driver be replaced by another.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If such a situation occurred, who would they turn to to be assigned a new driver?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: To the traffic and transportation department. In other words, my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you would then proceed to assign a new driver?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: That's correct, depending on the tasks, depending on the availability of the driver, depending on the senior officer who required a driver, depending on the driver's abilities, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let me put a specific question to you concerning Colonel Beara. If you remember, in the period between 1993 and the end of the war, was at any point of time a request submitted to your service for the driver to be changed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: A request for the replacement of a permanent driver was not received. I don't remember whether a substitute needed to be found because of absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkez, let us look at it realistically. This has been a long time ago. This has happened a long time ago, after all. How can you be so categorical in stating that such a request had not been received? What is the basis of your statement? What is the basis of the fact that you can make it statement with such certainty?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: As far as substituting a driver of the senior officers goes, I can say that such requests were very few and far between and were filed only when strictly necessary. Normally, such a senior officer and his driver would get close. And if the driver did his job correctly and properly, such requests would not be filed by the senior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: War is a tragic situation. Did there occur a situation where a driver fell ill or was killed or injured and required a replacement?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The drivers were not wounded or killed. There may have been illnesses, but they were quite short.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkez, in what way was the control of the vehicles assigned for permanent use to these senior officers carried out if there was any control?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: In addition to the traffic booklet, every vehicle had a vehicle work log where, on a monthly basis, records were kept on the amount of fuel used be and the kilometres of distance travelled in order to be able to make an analysis of the cost-effectiveness of the use of the vehicle at the end of the month or, conversely, of the possible abuse of its use.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The -- which data was entered into the vehicle work log of the vehicles assigned to the mentioned officers for permanent use?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The cover page of the vehicle work log had the name of the driver, the basic information about the vehicle, chassis, licence plate, type of fuel and the amount of fuel received for the particular month. Inside the work log the routes and the distances travelled were supposed to be entered. Now, when -- in the work logs used by these particular senior officers who had vehicles assign to them for permanent use, there only the distances travelled were entered and not the routes. This was done for security reasons, so that such confidential information may not be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The data you've just referred to, was this the subject of some regulation or rules dictating that this is the way the work logs should be kept, or did the situation vary on a case-to-case basis?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: This was not specifically regulated in the rules equally for all the vehicles. This was probably the practice introduced pursuant to a commander's order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What sort of information was written for the other type of vehicles that were assigned as needed for specific tasks?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: For these other vehicles which were used by different senior officers at different times every movement of the vehicle was specifically recorded in terms of the route taken, distances travelled, the destination, and of course they had to record the total amount of kilometres travelled on a particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you recall for some of the officers, and specifically for Ljubisa Beara, and for others if you remember, which vehicles were assigned to him in the period between 1993 and the end of the war? Did he have only one vehicle at his disposal that he used or were there several?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: In principle, every senior officer was assigned one passenger vehicle, except for the commander, a chief of staff, and Colonel Beara, who also had an all-terrain vehicle of the Puha make. 1

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Puh make, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you know which vehicles were use by some of the other officers?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Well, in principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we get the time frame?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I said that I was referring to the period between 1993 and the end of the war, which was the period during which Mr. Kerkez was the chief of the service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's not helpful. It's a long period of time, and if -- if we could focus on the time period in question, I think it would be a lot clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's up to you, Mr. Nikolic. At the end of the day you've brought this witness to give testimony, possibly to gain some advantage from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkez, in 1995 - let us focus on that year - what was the vehicle use by Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I've already said that drivers changed very rarely. Likewise, if there was no call for that, if the vehicles were not damaged or such like, I can claim with certainty that in 1995 Colonel Beara used that particular all-terrain vehicle and that he used the Golf 2 vehicle, the colour of which I don't remember. I do remember the make, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The subject of this trial are the events surrounding Srebrenica. Let me ask you this: In that period of time when the Srebrenica action was in course up until the end of the month of July, did the driver and the vehicle change?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I can reliably say that Colonel Beara had the same driver and the same vehicle and that he used them at a later date as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where were you during operation Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Before the commencement of the operation, that is to say between 28 June and 6 July, I was on furlough visiting my family. Later on I was at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So you went back to your duties on the 6th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Evidently, these are events that one remembers well because they are quite unfortunate. Let us focus on that particular period of time. At that time did Ljubisa Beara change his driver? Did he submit a request to that effect to your service, and did he change his vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: There were no such requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you find out about operation Srebrenica and in which way?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. It may be just a translation issue, but I -- this is being translated as Operation Srebrenica and that -- there's no -- I'm not familiar of any such operation, but if what you're saying is that the operation regarding Srebrenica, which may be -- I have no objection. But if there is an Operation Srebrenica, we need a foundation to establish it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic. It's not just --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. If your --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague is right. What I meant was operations around Srebrenica. I didn't mean it by way of an official name. I think we all know what we are talking about, and I hope that this is a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kerkez, there is no doubt in my mind that you found out about this operation around Srebrenica, so how did you find out?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Like most people I found out from the media. When it started, it was made public.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note. We can barely speaker due to background noise. Could all microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you arrived from vacation on the 6th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In which period did you find out about that? Was it as soon as you arrived? Could you please be more specific?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember exactly, but after two or three days, after my arrival, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: While you were away, while you were on vacation, who replaced you at your position?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I had two desk officers, Lieutenant Viskovic and Lieutenant Mirovic. One of them always had to be there at the department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I assume that when you returned it was customary that you would ask, like anyone would, what happened at work while you were away. So did you ask your assistant to report to you about what had been happening during the period while you were away?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Of course I expressed such an interest. Well, that was my duty, if I can put it that way. In addition to regular duties, there weren't any special requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Regardless of whether it was formal or informal, there certainly was information provided about the preceding period. Did he indicate to you any significant events that took place in your absence, I mean, requests vis-a-vis your service?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we take a break now? I'm going to move on to another subject that will certainly be important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Nikolic. We'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before continuing with the examination, I would like to inform you that in accordance with your suggestion we talked to our colleague from the OTP in relation to the testimony of witness Spiro Pereula. We agreed that the direct examination start today, and our colleagues from the OTP would like to cross-examine on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, but we probably won't get that far, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls is available to cross-examine today possibly, but he's not exactly sure yet, but I don't think we'll get that far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you both. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkez, let us now go back to the previous question regarding combat operations around Srebrenica, you said that you heard about them from the media. When did that happen? When did you receive this initial information about these combat operations?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I returned from Belgrade on the 6th in the afternoon. I heard the first information after two, three, or four days, as I said. After that, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In relation to that, did you make any comments with regard to these operations with your colleagues within the service or some other colleagues?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Well, of course, like concerning every new information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And did you learn anything?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No significant information apart from what I had already heard through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In preparation for this testimony we discussed this topic, and you said that after all, you did go towards Potocari. Could you please tell us why and how did this happen for you to set out towards Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading on a topic. There's just no reason to do that. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic. It is definitely leading. I mean, instead of him testifying where he went to and when, you're telling him. On the other hand, we all know that we are getting there because it was part of the information that was provided to the Prosecution, and which we heard before in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkez, did you go to Potocari at all?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Well, since I heard this information that these combat operations around Srebrenica had started, I also heard this information that evacuation had started, evacuation of the population from Srebrenica, and that this evacuation was taking place using the vehicles provided by the army. I do not recall the exact date, but I know that on the second day after that, with a view to receiving information or, rather, seeing whether any assistance was needed by the transportation organ of the Drina Corps and to see whether they had enough vehicles and whether any intervention was needed, I went to the spot to see for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In your answer you said that you heard that evacuation was taking place using vehicles provided by the army. Could you please specify? What was your knowledge exactly as to how the army had provided this -- or, rather, from that point of view did your service provide these vehicles and plan for the use of these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: That is why I went on that second day to Potocari, because there weren't any requests, and my department had not provided any kind of transportation vehicles for this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where did you set out from?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Rado Vickovic, my assistant, drove the vehicle and I was there with Colonel Simovic and I set out sometime during the morning on that day from Han Pijesak, that is to say from the logistics sector -- or, rather, from the locality where my service was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Was the headquarters of your service in Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The logistics sector and the sector for morale had its headquarters at the hotel in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Tell me, with these three colleagues you set out. Could you describe the road you took from Han Pijesak to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Well, the only road that exists is Han Pijesak-Vlasenica-Milici-Konjevic Polje-Bratunac, and towards Srebrenica to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Along that road to Potocari did you notice -- or, rather, did you see any combat operations?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Then along that road I did not notice any, although I did hear gunfire from afar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you arrive in Potocari, at what time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Sometime around noon. Was it a few minutes or after, that's not something I can say with any degree of certainty now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe what it was that you saw in Potocari and who you found there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: When I arrived in Potocari I observed a number of vehicles lined up and a larger presence of the Muslim population, including women, children, young men, and the elderly who were boarding the column of vehicles. I also came across units of the civilian police, army units, and -- and a group of UNPROFOR soldiers securing the whole process of boarding the buses, the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Who did you see of the senior officers there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Since the army was present there was also a number of senior officers there who I knew by sight from the Drina Corps. I only knew the chief of the transportation service, Colonel Krsmanovic by name. I approached him and talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What was it that you talked about with Mr. Krsmanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The conversation had to do with the transportation effort, whether there were enough transportation resources and whether there were any difficulties. His response was that everything had been provided for and that no assistance was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were there many vehicles there, or was it the usual number of vehicles that the army normally required?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: In addition to military vehicles who were normally rather small, there were military buses, and there were also trailer trucks with civilian licence plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss the large presence of vehicles there since, as you say, the Main Staff had not received any requests for vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Of course. Having observed the vehicles there, I asked how they came to be there. I was told that civilian vehicles had been requisitioned, commandeered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. He never said the Main Staff never received any requests. He said something about him not receiving requests or his unit, but the main -- well, the Main Staff is bigger, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic. That seems to be correct. I don't recall the witness having brought in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Your Honours, but he talked about his service, and he explained the nature and the duties of his service within the Main Staff. If I remember correctly, he talked about his service, conduct, and planning upon the order or request from one of the units. That's why I put the question as I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the location?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: For the maximum of 20 to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where did you head next?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I went back to the Main Staff along the same route.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you describe your journey back to the headquarters in Han Pijesak? Did you happen to come across the columns on your way and were there any combat activities along the way?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: As I was on my way back on the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road, we were nearing Konjevic Polje when I caught up along the road with groups of soldiers whom I recognised as members of the Muslim army. They were coming out of the forest in groups of a number of soldiers. Some of them carried weapons, others didn't. Some of them were going -- or moving on their own and others were led by our soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What was your reaction to such a scene?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I assumed that they were attempting to reach the Muslim-controlled territory in the direction of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How far along your way did you notice these individual groups of men?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: All the way until the crossroads between Zvornik and Han Pijesak and Bratunac-Konjevic Polje. In other words, I would see them all the way to the crossroads. Beyond that from Konjevic Polje towards Kasaba, the distance is of some 100 metres, on the roadside where there was a football pitch I noticed a group of Muslim soldiers seated on the grass of the football pitch. At the edge of the football pitch there was a reception point. There were several desks there, and members of -- or soldiers of the VRS seated at the desks registering the soldiers who were there, the soldiers having been disarmed and their name placed on the record would be taken to join the others seated in the centre of the football pitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Since the football pitch is some two metres away from the road, we pulled over on the roadside close to the reception point and stayed there for some two to three minutes to take in what was going on, because could I not recognise the senior soldiers who were there. We then resumed our trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where did you go to next?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Toward headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: In Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me make a correction, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On page 3, lines 5 and 6, let us clarify where the headquarters of your service was and what the name of the service was.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The headquarters of the logistics sector with all the attendant services was at a hotel in Han Pijesak. The exact title is the Department of the Traffic and Transportation Service in the Sector of Logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In addition to your sector, were there other sectors represented there as well?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Of course. The logistics centre comprised several departments; namely, technical services, quartermaster services, transportation services, construction services, Medical Corps services, and veterinarian services.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It was necessary for us to intervene and to go back to that point in the transcript in order to clarify where the headquarters of your service was. Let us go back to where we left off. Where did you head to next, and when did you return to your headquarters in Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: If I was in Potocari at around 1200 hours and stayed there for roughly half an hour, the trip from Potocari to Han Pijesak took an hour and a half roughly. So it could have been past 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were the two colleagues of yours with you throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkez, when we spoke of the automobile unit at the outset, I mentioned Mr. Beara and his driver. How long have you known Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I got to know him when I joined the Main Staff. In other words, in September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Along the Han Pijesak-Potocari road and on your way back in Potocari or at any point at any section of the road, did you come across Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No. I claim with certainty that I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: 1993 was a long time ago, but nevertheless can you tell us and describe for us the physical appearance of Colonel Beara? If you can, what you remember of his physical appearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. McCloskey, time frame?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think there is -- it may just be a typing mistake, because we see 1993 on the thing, and again if that's the time frame, fine, but 1995, I think would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you interested in 1993 or 1995, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in 1995, or more precisely, the trip to Potocari and back. However, I mentioned 1993 in order for the witness to be able to tell us since when he had known Mr. Beara so that we could gauge how realistic his description of Colonel Beara is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you answer the question, please, if you can?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Colonel Beara was a tall man, some 190 centimetres. He was always grey, but he didn't have a receding hairline as he does now, and of medium build.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kerkez. I have completed my cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Examination, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you so much, Mr. Nicholls -- Mr. Nikolic. Now, Mr. Zivanovic, you had asked for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will not cross-examine this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Ms. Nikolic, you had asked for a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Lazarevic, you had asked for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I hope I will make it in ten minutes. I will have some cross-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel. My name is Aleksandar Lazarevic and together with my colleagues I represent Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin. I should like to put a couple of questions to you. The examination won't be long, but it will have to do with some matters from the examination-in-chief, and it will serve to clarify some matters. In the course of your evidence today you said at what time and on what day you were present in Potocari and what you had occasion to see. I would like to put a number of questions to you on that score. You said that when you observed the larger group of civilians, women, children, and others in Potocari, the civilian police and the army helped evacuate them. So I'll put a couple of questions about that. When you said the civilian police, the reason for you saying that is that you were able to see that quite clearly on the basis of their uniforms. They had blue uniforms, did they not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You were also able to observe the civilian police vehicles, white in colour, that were present in Potocari at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: During that brief stay of yours, you said it lasted some 20 to 30 minutes, you had occasion to see UNPROFOR forces mingling with the civilian police, the army, and the refugees there, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes. A number of them. It was not a large unit, put it that way. It was more of a patrol, a group of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You were also able to observe that UNPROFOR members, and I don't think that's contested, that they were members of the DutchBat, that UNPROFOR members were also taking part in the evacuation effort because they were assisting the population boarding the buses in an orderly fashion so as to prevent chaos. Were you able to observe something like that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes. Probably there very presence there helped avert any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question in connection with this. During this brief stay in Potocari, did you observe any sort of indecent conduct or misconduct on the part of the -- these units vis-a-vis the general population, that they beat them up, insulted them, used derogatory language, or force them to board the buses or anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No, I did not observe anything that would resemble that. The evacuation was taking its course in an orderly fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you told us you met Colonel Krsmanovic from the Drina Corps on that occasion. You had a brief conversation with him. In the course of the conversation did Colonel Krsmanovic tell you who had secured the fuel necessary for the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: He did. I was told that the fuel had not been received from the Main Staff, or that is to say from the army of the -- of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me put it differently. Did you receive information that the United Nations, or, rather, the UNPROFOR forces had secured fuel for that operation? Was that the sort of information you received?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I can't be sure. I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You also testified that you travelled along the road from Potocari to Bratunac, and then you said that you proceeded from Bratunac all the way to an intersection at Konjevic Polje. You said that on your way you noticed a larger and smaller groups of Muslims, some armed, others unarmed, who were coming down the slope and surrendering to the members of the VRS. Did you on that occasion observe any sort of misconduct by any of the members of the VRS as you saw them on the roadside?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No. I believe that what I was able to observe was proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would just like the witness to be shown another document that we will be using.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: However, before that I would like to put another question to you. Radoslav Jankovic, is that a name that rings a bell to you? Colonel Radoslav Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Jankovic? No. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Radoslav Jankovic, to the best of our knowledge, was on the intelligence organ of the Main Staff. Perhaps that may assist you in remembering?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: It depends on the period involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm going to clarify that a bit now when we look at this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up in e-court 5D5113.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm being informed that this document doesn't show up on e-court. Are you -- are you sure about the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document is already admitted into evidence for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 5DP, 5DP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, could you please have a look at this document. I assume that you haven't seen it until now, so you may need some time in order to familiarise yourself with the content. On the right-hand side you have the document in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Could it please be zoomed in a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think that will be feasible. Yes, see? Did you now have occasion at that familiarise yourself with it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you see in this document Colonel Radoslav Jankovic reports that on the 13th of July, 1995, at 2000 hours the evacuation of the entire Muslim population from the former enclave of Srebrenica was completed. Does this perhaps jog your memory? Can you now perhaps remember who Mr. Jankovic was?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Madam Fauveau? No cross?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic, you asked for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel. My name is Dragan Krgovic, and on behalf of the Defence of General Gvero, I'm going to put a few questions to you in relation to your testimony here today. In your response to my learned friend Mr. Nikolic's question, you mentioned a few names of drivers who drove certain people from the Main Staff. I'm going to ask you specifically about my client. In 1995, who were the people who drove General Gvero, if you remember? You mentioned a name, Zoranovic. Is this Nedeljko Zoranovic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from Zoranovic did any other drivers drive General Gvero at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: It was -- I don't known whether it was in that period.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I know that General Gvero was driven by two other drivers. Now, whether that was precisely in that period, that is something I'm not quite sure of. One is Rajak, and one is Macanovic or, rather, the other one is Macanovic. Now, was it precisely in that period of time, I cannot assert that with 100 per cent certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember which vehicle was use the by General Gvero in 1995? According to the information I have, he used an Opel car.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: It was the driver who drove the general. General Gvero did have an Opel. That is correct. One was Vectra, but the other one I'm not sure because one of the two was damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that General Gvero in the beginning of March, 1995, had a car accident with one of these vehicles and that he was injured in the accident?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: This rarely happens, especially with ranking officers, so I remember this very well. It was the Opel Vectra, and that is true. That did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The vehicle was repaired after that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes, after a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where the vehicle had been repaired?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but I think it was at a service station in Serbia. Loznica, Mali Zvornik, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall perhaps what the name was of the service station or the name of the man or the nickname of the man who repaired the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I don't remember the name, but I think that the service station was called Lamela.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Another question. Do you remember the colour of the vehicle driven by General Gvero? According to the information that I have, the vehicle driven by General Gvero after this accident was light green.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes, that was the colour of that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did General Gvero ever drive a black vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of him taking some other vehicle at some points in time? As far as I know that was not the case, that some officer would take another officers's car without that being recorded by your service.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: If another vehicle was being used, that had to be with my knowledge because the driver would have to come with the vehicle, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995 you are not aware of any such case with General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No, I do not recall. I don't think that any such thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Haynes, Mr. Sarapa, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: A few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. [No interpretation] ... your question if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't -- okay. I don't know, but we didn't have interpretation of what you were saying, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I put another question that I omitted to put a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
