utterances.text: The vehicles that General Gvero used, did they have any radio equipment in them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No. No. It was only the commander and the chief of staff that had such equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning I'm Mr. Djordje Sarapa on Defence team of Vinko Pandurevic. I'm going to put a few questions to you. Most of them will be very brief and you will be able to them by a simple yes or no. Can you please tell me, your superior was the assistant logistics commander, right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: As for responsibility for fuel supplies and the use of fuel -- use of fuel -- I just need to wait for a second. As for responsibility for fuel supplies, that was under the technical service; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Generally at a unit level, the Main Staff, the corps, brigades, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: In view of the position that you held over a few years, could you describe for us briefly how the army of Republika Srpska was supplied with fuel?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Since in principle when fuel arrives in bases and is allocated to specific units, I wanted it to be used in an economical way. The army was supplied by fuel mostly through purchases from manufacturers or traders in the republic or outside the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about the distribution of fuel in units?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The distribution of fuel was carried out by the logistics sector or, rather, the technical service depending on the tasks that would follow and, of course, the orders of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. While responding to Mr. Nikolic's questions you mentioned the Automobile Battalion. It was stationed in Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: That was true in July 1995 as well, right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you remember who commanded the battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The battalion commander at the time was Lieutenant Radakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume that you knew Mr. Radisav Pantic, chief of the transportation service of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I assume that you had personal contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: That's right, during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Outside the regular chain of command, you sometimes give Pantic help and did he help you out too?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could you briefly explain to us how that happened and in what cases, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Well, there were a few such cases, if I can put it that way. However, this had to do with the use of battalion vehicles that was under the command of the Main Staff. If I can put it this way: The vehicles were located right by the brigade command. In order to simplify the procedure of use, then sometimes, if I can put it that way, sometimes the corps level was skipped. So Pantic would directly address me instead of going through the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us -- if we look at a particular document, an order or a document of any kind, what does it mean when it says "na znande," "for the knowledge of," literally?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Well, that means that the command is being informed, or some organ of a particular piece of information or an order, if I can put it that way, that does not pertain to them directly, but it does pertain to their unit. So whoever is addressing the order is informing the superior about that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: On direct examination you mentioned the procedure whereby drivers were selected for individual senior officers. Can you tell us, did the security organs have a role to play in the selection of drivers?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes. They were entitled to choose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: You mean for themselves? I believe we misunderstand each other. What I'd like to know is the whether you have any knowledge about the possible role of the security organ in the selection of a driver for, let's say, a commander or a chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Of course. They had the duty to vet a given individual and see if he or she was suitable for the job because it had to be the sort of person who could maintain confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can document P295 be shown. Pages 603 and 604, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you see it on your screen, Mr. Kerkez?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes. This is the vehicle work log.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Let's disregard the name and other data contained here. Generally speaking, I would like you to help us with how a vehicle work log was fill out. We have the full name of the driver, and then we have the information about the fuel, and then the first line to the left, date. Was one supposed to place the date when fuel and lubricants were taken?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes, because this particular box was supposed to be filled out by the person serving fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. To the far right it says signature of the operator or person handling something. Who did that refer to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: To the person issuing fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I suppose the signature should be placed on the same day as the fuel is being distributed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Can we turn to the following page, please. It says the -- the running of the work order of the vehicle, machinery or device. And then we have the left column of the date. Who fills out that column?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Both the date and the route taken?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: When is the driver supposed to fill out the date and the route?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: As he sets out for his assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: On the day the assignment is supposed to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Then we have the initial status in kilometres. Who is supposed to fill this out?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The driver. He is supposed to copy the figure indicating kilometres at the beginning of the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And the routes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Well, everything that pertains to this matter, save for the last column which is to be signed by the user of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And that is who?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Well, the person who the driver drove or worked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. You've given me the answers I was interested in. I thank you for that. And I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. My name is Peter McCloskey --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- and I represent the Office of the Prosecutor. I'll be asking you a few questions this morning and this afternoon. First on a topic you just mentioned. How is it that you know anything or are involved with fuel?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: That's my profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain that in more detail, where fuel fits into your job, especially in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The consumption of fuel by a vehicle is one of the indicators of the exploitation and the cost-effectiveness of a job, and it falls under one of the tasks of the transportation service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So that -- it's your job to know about shipments of fuel across corps lines to various units, things like that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Essentially, yes, although that is the duty of the technical service. The quantities and times of shipment fall within the responsibility of the technical service. I am only supposed to use the fuel economically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you should know about large amounts of fuel that are sent to various operations to see to it that it can be used economically?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You had mentioned that you got your supplies of fuel from various places inside the republic. You also mentioned you, of course, got it outside the republic. When you say getting fuel outside the republic, where are you referring to? And I'm mostly talking about 1995.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I knew of the movement of fuel from the point the fuel reached the logistics base and was supposed to be distributed to units. How the fuel reached the base was the responsibility of the technical service. Still, I was familiar with the way the bases were supplied in general terms but not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question was, sir, where -- you said the fuel came from outside the republic. Can you tell me where?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: That piece of information is known, but I don't know exactly where from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't need to be exact. Where were you getting most of your fuel, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Believe me that this was the responsibility of the technical service, and I cannot state this with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where do you think you were getting most of your fuel from in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau, why?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because this question is a speculative one. The witness apparently does not know where from exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He either knows or he doesn't, I think. I mean, if he doesn't, obviously he's not to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is cross-examination. It's a perfectly fair question, especially given the fact that I think everyone in the world knows where the fuel came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although this was not my responsibility, every single senior officer of the army knew that the only source of supply was Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. That wasn't -- shouldn't be that hard, okay? And who in Serbia was the principal provider that is known to every senior officer in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection once again, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the relevance of this question in this trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I didn't bring up fuel, Mr. President. This is an issue that's been brought up. He testified fuel was coming from the inside and outside. I think the credibility is an issue, and I think fuel is a big issue, especially regarding what he had said about his involvement in this operation. Fuel is a massive issue, and these objections are -- well, I won't say what they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, my objection was not about fuel. It was about the responsibility in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not concerned about the cost of fuel. I'm concerned about responsibility, of course, Mr. President, as is this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's close it here. Let me consult with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can't see any validity to your objection, Madam Fauveau. It's a question that completely relates to the subject matter of this person's -- of this witness's testimony. So let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, was the VJ providing the VRS with fuel in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I said that the technical service supplied bases with fuel, and I don't know where they obtained it from although it was general knowledge that it came from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was it also general knowledge that it came from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You have no knowledge at all whether the VJ was supporting the VRS in the provisions of fuel? You've just said that fuel was your profession, part of your profession. And, sir, I remind you you are under oath.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I know that, and I repeat, I was aware of what happened to fuel as it reached bases from where it was distributed to various units. How fuel reached bases is something I don't have specific information about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Weren't you responsible for fuel all over the areas controlled by the -- the VRS? All the corps areas of responsibility, those were -- that was your area of fuel and fuel transport; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: That's correct. Only within the army, but not -- I wasn't concerned with how and from whom fuel was procured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, who arranged for the transport of the fuel that came from Serbia to you? Were the -- was the VJ or the Serbs always generous enough to supply their own vehicles and bring it in their own trucks? Or didn't sometimes you have to go over and get some yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I personally never did. I was concerned with organisation, but I only knew where the fuel was supposed to be taken from and to where. For the rest, I wasn't informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you saying you have no knowledge whatsoever of any VRS transportation assets ever going to Serbia to get fuel?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The army vehicles were not used because the army did not have large capacity tanks, tank trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you do know the kinds of vehicles that went to get fuel. What vehicles went to get fuel from Serbia? Talk to us about these large capacity tank trucks, and we won't need to spend very long if you just tell us. These are quick and easy questions.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: It is an easy question. In order for a certain quantity or amount of fuel to be transported, the appropriate vehicle for that, a tank truck or a cistern is required. If the vehicle is supposed to cover larger distances, it is only logical to use a vehicle of higher tonnage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course. And your -- the logistics section was involved in the -- as you call it, the organising and the planning and the carrying out of the transport of the trucks over to Serbia and the transport of the fuel back, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes. They were large capacity tank trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And your unit at the Main Staff was responsible for seeing to it that they got to Serbia and got back as you've described your job, organising, planning, carrying out.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you said you were involved -- and I won't stay on this forever, but you said you were involved in helping what we're all thinking about these days, conserve or figure out fuel. Can you give me an estimate, just a very rough estimate, of how many tonnes of fuel came from Serbia, to your knowledge, that your unit was involved in in 1995? Just roughly.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: It was not my task to keep fuel. It was the responsibility of the logistics bases, and they kept track of how many tons of fuel they had. I have no idea about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember your answer to my question earlier? You said it was -- it wasn't your job to actually transport. I think it was to keep track of it. But you don't know how -- you don't have any estimate at all?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: It was not my task to keep a record of the amount of fuel. My task was to make sure that the fuel used by units was used economically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Who, if anyone, in the Ministry of Defence did you consult with in your job in receiving fuel from Serbia and making sure that it was dealt with economically? I'm talking about the RS Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I didn't have a direct connection with the Ministry of Defence. It was the Main Staff who had that, or to be precise, the logistics sector. Therefore, I have no idea in what way the fuel was procured. My task was to receive a specific request and to make sure that the request is acted upon. That's to say that certain transportation is carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- let me ask you about a specific one. That's go to 65 ter number 42. A copy of that will come up on your screen. I can give you a hard copy. That might be helpful. If I could give you a hard copy. That's hard to read, I've got to tell you. This is a -- you can try to read it there, sir, but let me... thank you. This is a document from the Main Staff, from the Technical Division that you've talked about, on 14 September 1995. "Attention, command of the 35th logistics base, Drina Corps command (for information) 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade (for information)," and you've told us what that means. "Pursuant to the order of the commander of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska immediately issue the following quantity of fuel to the Drina Corps command: D-2, 5.000 litres. "The above quantity of fuel will be used for engineering works ..." and it goes on. Now, who is Colonel Zarko Ljubojecic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: He was a colleague who was the chief of the technical division of the logistics sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So is this a rather large amount of fuel?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No. It's a very small quantity 5.000 litres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter number 41. Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No. This was sent directly to the unit, and I didn't have anything to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, how did you know it was sent directly to the unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: You can see it in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sent from where?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: It was sent from the Main Staff, from the technical division of the logistics sector to the 35th logistics base, stating that the unit would take the stated amount of fuel directly from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So where is the fuel depot that you're talking about in relation to Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The fuel was to be taken from the 35th logistics base in Bijeljina. The 35th logistics base is in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Take a look at this other document that is now up on the screen. I think that one should be easier to read. And I won't read it all out. We can see that this is referring to the same date. Five tons of D-2. "The logistics sector of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska shall deliver to the standard barracks in Zvornik." Are you aware that General Mladic issued this order?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No. I wasn't aware of it because it didn't go through me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fuel is your profession. You didn't have to look after what happened this fuel, what happened to the remaining fuel, where it went to so you could incorporate it into the fuel reserves that you would be sending out to various corps? This is 5.000 litres that was never on your radar screen?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: If I may clarify. This same order is identical. It is just that General Mladic approved the stated quantity, whereas the other order orders the unit to take over that same stated amount of fuel from that logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand. And you're as equally unknowledgeable about General Mladic and this 5000 tonnes as you are -- or 500 tonnes as you were the previous document?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Every document that I did not sign or every document that did not pertain to transportation only was outside of my knowledge. I could not have known about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, okay. Let's set aside fuel. You were also responsible for trucks, big trucks, buses, for big Main Staff operations, right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Only if the vehicles were from a Main Staff unit. If the vehicles were part of a corps, then they were no longer my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, did you assist the 10th Sabotage Detachment of the Main Staff get to the Srebrenica attack area on or around 8, 9 July, 1995 when you were back in the office from your holiday? You've heard of them, haven't you, the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I've already told your colleague that we in the Main Staff did not receive a single request for any job that would do -- would have to do with transportation in relation to any unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we'll get into that a little bit more as we get to the time frame. Were you aware of the acquiring of large numbers -- it's hard to say, 15, 20 very large trucks, big dump trucks, the kind that they haul bauxite around in from mid-September to roughly mid-October for a large transportation of materiel, men and materiel in the area of the Zvornik and Bratunac Brigades? Huge operation, took several days, drove through the night doing it, lots and lots of fuel had to be used. You must have know what I'm talking about. It was a Main Staff operation.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: One such request was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not sure what the Prosecutor is relying on when he says that it was a big operation or that it was conducted by the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you wish to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I probably shouldn't be commenting in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkez, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A little. Then I think you better leave the courtroom a little bit, for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sure I don't need to explain to the Court the size of the reburial operation. It was massive to say the least. We all remember the dates. I think we remember when the Zvornik Brigade officer suddenly told us all about it for the first time and the involvement of people. It went from Zvornik to the areas around Snagovo, and it went from Glogova to the areas south of Srebrenica. It was a very large operation. It went through the night. You may recall the -- well, I won't get into the grim evidence associated with it. And the part about the Main Staff, you may recall the notes of the command staff of the Bratunac Brigade in October of 1995 where Momir Nikolic makes a note, and this is during a time period where we have provided aerial imagery showing the disturbed earth. The note from the command staff that Momir Nikolic motes that asenacija is being done by orders of Main Staff. That's the basis of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed. Let's bring the witness in. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before the witness is brought back in, maybe the Prosecutor could state what is it about exactly, because one could think that it was about a military operation in September and October of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I think he's made that clear now, no? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm being tricky. I don't want to give it away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may need to go back to page 60, lines 1 to 7 if you wish to repeat your question. Otherwise rephrase it. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were in the process of answering the question. You said, I'd think you'd known about something and then you were interrupted, can you tell us what it was that you were telling us?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I wished to say that no such request had ever reached me or the Main Staff, or had I ever heard of such an operation like what you have referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you -- you can't really speak for the whole Main Staff, can you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I cannot. I'm speaking in my own name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And if hundreds and hundreds of litres of fuel was used for that job, you should have known about it; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No. Fuel -- well, you've seen that fuel is directly given by the army commander, that is to say the quantity concerned. I don't think you understand. The my obligation is to check how the fuel is being used. It is not that I provide fuel for the implementation of tasks or operations. That is the duty of the technical service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm reminded you started your question [sic] with "One such request was," and then you were interrupted. And that's on page 60, line 8. Do you want to finish that thought?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I think that I said no such request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps. Thanks. Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's break time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, the other day we were in court and we had a document where there was a mention of a person from the Main Staff. This was a document from 5 August. It was an intercepted conversation, and there was a person written down here called Lieutenant Colonel Stevanovic. Do you know a Lieutenant Colonel Stevanovic? May have been in the section that approved passes, press passes, things like that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter number 3178. This is a Main Staff personnel employment record. And if we could first go to -- if we could go to page -- well, let's let the witness see the first page so he can just get an idea what that looks like. Okay. So we see Main Staff, Glavni Stab VRS. And if we could go to page -- let's start with page 19, if you can find that. And you can see -- that's your name right up there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who's the person above your name on this document?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Colonel Ostoja Stijepic. That is a Colonel who held this post before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So let's now go to page 13 of the list. I'm sorry, perhaps you can help me here. What section is this that we see there at the top and those first few names, Vidoje and Slobodan? What section is that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Do you mean the first three men?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, and their section.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: These men worked in the section for morale, General Gvero's section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then can we -- let's go down to the -- oh, not too much, sorry. Right there. That's fine. Boris Stankovic, who is that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then we see that Vasilija Stevanovic, and what's the rank of that Stevanovic according to this document?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I don't remember him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right. But can you -- according to the document, can you tell us what the rank is?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: According to what is written here, lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then if we go over to the far right, we see a date area. This is all handwritten. And this is -- it's 31 July '95; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Does seeing that help -- help your recollection at all of this guy? The Main Staff wasn't a very big outfit.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes, but -- but not everybody was at the same location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where were Gvero's people on this list in July '95? You were at this hotel in Han Pijesak; right? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: As far as I know, part of them were in Crna Rijeka, and part of them were in a building that was not the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where was Gvero? Where did he have his office, July '95?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: In July '95, in principle he was in is Crna Rijeka. However, he spent a certain period of time at the hotel. As for the exact time, I cannot say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Now, you told us that you got back from holiday on the 6th of July, 1995, and you also told us that you didn't hear about anything to do with the Srebrenica operation until you heard it on the media. What was the first thing you say you heard about the Srebrenica operation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: It is correct that I had not had any information until this was made public through the media. As far as I can remember, what was published was that fighting had started around the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you first start communicating with people from the Srebrenica area, like Krsmanovic or others, in doing your job to help assist that operation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask it again. But let me before I -- let me try to have you clear something up. It wasn't really clear to me when you testified what day you actually went to Potocari. Can you try to sort that out for us? I mean, in relation to something.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Well, I remember that it was -- I mean, the second day when the evacuation of the population started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So the second day of what? I mean, not of -- I'm not talking about the month. The second day of evacuation, the second day of something else? What do you mean when you say "the second day"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The previous day I heard again through the media that the evacuation of the civilian population had started from the town of Srebrenica, and I left on the following day to see how all of this was developing and whether any assistance was needed perhaps. The transport service from the Drina Corps, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you say you heard about the evacuation of the population on the first day, and I think everyone will agree, just to clarify the record, that the first day of the evacuation was the 12th of July. So if you don't mind, I'll say the 12th. Tell me, what did you learn was happening on the 12th of July and from what source in particular, as best as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Since this operation was known of earlier on, that is to say fighting had already started and so on and so forth, on that day, well, I don't remember the exact date, but if you say that it was the 12th, then say in the afternoon, sometime in the afternoon hours, I heard through the media, as I've already said, that people started evacuating from Srebrenica, and they were being transported towards Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you -- had you been at work full time from the 6th of July through the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Surely you were aware of the massive effort to get buses and fuel together to be able to get those civilian population folks over to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a leading question in view of the fact that the witness has already answered this question unequivocally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are on cross, and on cross leading questions are permitted to start with. Secondly, do you wish, Mr. McCloskey, to rebut the allegation that the witness has already answered this question, unequivocally?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think he's answered it unequivocally. And, Mr. President, in cross-examination sometimes it's appropriate to ask the same question twice, especially a question as fundamental as he's in his office from 6th to the 12th of July in the -- in his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sometimes even in direct. Let's proceed. Mr. Kerkez, please, if you could please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it was -- the question was surely you became aware sometime between the 6th and the 12th of the effort on the VRS to get buses and trucks and fuel to Bratunac and Potocari to help get those civilians over to the Muslim-held territory.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I've already told your colleague my service, my department, did not receive a single request from any quarters to provide any sort of vehicle, not even for that specific task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, okay, but how about did you know about the need for buses, that the VRS was looking for buses and fuel? Your job is fuel, if you told us. Your job is buses and trucks and transport, and this court has heard a lot of information about buses and trucks coming from all over Bosnia. You weren't aware of that at all?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: That, even if it was done, it was done without the knowledge of the Main Staff. Most probably the unit which implemented it did so on the orders from an individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? What individual? Do you think Vinko Pandurevic can do this on his own?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, Ms. Nikolic -- one moment, Mr. Kerkez. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it was the interpretation that caused the problem. The witness said "units" and not "individuals."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to confirm that, but Mr. McCloskey, assuming that Ms. Nikolic is right, do you wish to put another question or move to your next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Most probably the unit which implemented it did so on the orders from a unit. I think I would put my faith in the interpreters on that one, but I think we can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If any of the -- of the interpreters could help us, I think that would be useful. What did the witness say?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter interpreted the way she heard at the time. It's difficult for me to go back and confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's not a big deal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 156.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I know this happened a while back but when did you first speak to the Beara team and actually start providing information and doing, you know, recollecting what happened?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Are you referring to Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, to Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Nikolic, you know, who you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Meek, others on the team.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The first time was in Belgrade about a month ago with the lawyer, Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember Mr. Stanic's entire name?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Not at this moment, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you tell him basically what you've told us today in court?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: We talked about the events that occurred at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Anything that you told them then in Belgrade that is different than what you've told us today?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did anybody write down anything that you said?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Maybe he did in some personal -- well, maybe just an outline or whatever. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, anything that you got to see to kind of read back to check that it was what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about when you were hear in The Hague? It's normal to talk with the people again before you come in to testify. Did you have a chance to talk with someone from -- Mr. Nikolic, or Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did he show you anything to read, any -- anything to help refresh your recollection during that time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No. We just talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you add anything new or change anything from what you said in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No. In principle, everything was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look at this document. You've been talking about that you are a request receiver, and you're talking about your responsibility for buses and fuel. You were in the office on the 12th of July, I think you've told us, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And okay. And here we have a request from the command of the Drina Corps, dated 12 July. We see it's the time delivered looks like it's in the morning around 10.00, 10.20, something like that. And it says: "To the VRS Main Staff." And the PKM, what's the PKM.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: The rear command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: At the hotel in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your offices?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it says: "Pursuant to the VRS commander's order to provide 50 buses for evacuation from the Srebrenica enclave, we hereby ask you for additional approval of the following types and quantities." You've got fuel and maybe a diesel. We've got petrol. And then we go on and it talks about buses. They're supposed to go from these -- all these municipalities all over the place, and the final destination isn't really -- is unknown. Does this help refresh your recollection? And take your time, sir, and think about it. It's important. You're not on trial here.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I understand. This is a request of the commander of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic. He is asking for additional quantities of fuel. So this falls under the technical service, not the transport service. As regards buses, he is asking -- well, from these places, these are civilian buses, to make their mobilisation possible. That's not the work of the traffic and transportation service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, who -- who at the hotel, at the rear command post, is supposed to deal with this for vehicles and the transport of vehicles if it's not you or your service?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: It's for vehicles that are not within the military. It is under the Ministry of the Defence, or, rather, the organ for organisation and mobilisation in the Main Staff. That is to say, mobilised vehicles. That is to say, those that are not within the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you get involved in helping get any vehicles or buses to the area of Bratunac on the 12th or 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No, and I was not aware of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter number 3574. Sir, were you aware that the Muslim army was listening to conversations from Han Pijesak throughout the zone of responsibility of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No security guy ever told you to be careful on what you say on the radio, the Muslims are listening?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Well, yes, I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sure. Okay. We have an intercept here from 12 July, and according to the Muslims it's between Lieutenant Colonel Kerkez, traffic, and an unidentified male X, and the conversation went as follows: "Hello, Lieutenant Colonel Kerkez from traffic speaking." X says: "Yes." Then Kerkez says: "The following, say, a few trailer trucks needed to be engaged in the direction down towards Bratunac." X says: "Yes, they're engaged." Kerkez says: "Have they left already?" X says: "They're leaving." Kerkez says: "Good. So there's no problem." X says: "None." Then Kerkez says, and it's our position, sir, that this is you saying this: "Listen, two buses will report to you from the Eastern Bosnia Corps command with registration plates BN," and then the numbers, "for the same task. Have them tanked up a bit as well and that there." X says: "Okay. Understood. Carry on." What task were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't remember. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't remember what? You don't remember what this task was, or you don't even remember that you ever -- you were ever engaged in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember the conversation, and I don't remember the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As Mr. Nikolic said in his questioning to you, these were very memorable events, and he said that because they were memorable you remembered things. You have told us you went to Potocari the next day on the 13th. Surely, sir, now that you've had a chance to think about this, you remember helping organise the buses, the fuel to Bratunac, Potocari.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this only has to do with the few vehicles. I don't know what this is all about and what the task was. Really, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You say you went to Potocari the next day. Did you see the military-aged men getting separated from their families?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I didn't see either the military-aged men and -- or was there ever such an event there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're telling us today that there was never an event in Potocari. There was no military-aged men that were ever separated from their families. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No. I told you that at the time I was there I didn't see that event, that's to say, the separation of the military-aged men from their families, nor did I observe such men. There were women, children, the elderly aged around 70, and some young boys aged 15, 16. I didn't see any military-aged men save for my trip back when I saw them surrender there or being taken prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I want to show you some video film that was shot at the time in the afternoon of 13 July, and we'll play that. Take a look at it, see if it helps refresh your recollection. It's 65 ter 2047. And did you know a senior MUP officer named Ljubisa [Realtime transcript read in error "Ljubomir"] Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Only by name. Personally, no, we didn't come across each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment on this. I heard you -- correct me if I am wrong, Mr. McCloskey. In the transcript we have "Ljubomir." I heard you say "Ljubisa."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's actually perhaps an issue in dispute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I'm just asking you because I heard you say "Ljubisa" but the transcript says "Ljubomir."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ah, the transcript should say Ljubisa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I had asked the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I know him as both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that there is an allegation that both existed, but I'm pointing this out because the transcript should reflect what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the witness now knows that he is being directed to answer in relation to a person Ljubisa Borovcanin and not Ljubomir Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you said you had heard of him by name back in 1995, did you -- had -- had you heard of him by name?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I heard the name, and I know that he worked on some security tasks in the civilian police. I don't know exactly what.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's -- let's take a look at this -- this video and I'll ask you a question or two about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I don't know which particular part of the video Mr. McCloskey wants to play, but I have some assumption, and I would like to make a submission which wouldn't be appropriate in front of the witness since he understands --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Perfectly understandable. Mr. Kerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just in order to be fair to the witness, I understand that Mr. McCloskey's entitled to put to the witness whatever he deems appropriate in his cross-examination, but it is my understanding that this witness testified that he was there at noon, and according to the evidence and according to some -- well, some time which can be seen on this video, it was shooted later, couple of hours later. So I don't know how would it help to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, but if I am reading Mr. McCloskey right, that has got nothing to do with it, but Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this -- I don't have a video at noon, otherwise I'd probably show that one to him, but this is, I think, close enough for my purposes. I'm going to show him these men jammed into the white house, and I'm thinking at noon there's still men in that white house, maybe not as many. But I think it's a relevant enough -- and we see Mr. Borovcanin standing in front of the white house, and so that's, you know, I thought I'd ask if I knew him first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly what I thought you would say to be honest. Let's -- let's proceed and then we see how it turns out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, we're going to show you something that was right along that main road where all those people you've described were -- were huddling around, and I want to see if this kind of rings any bells for you, if -- something that you might have seen. And there's a big house in this picture. Okay? Let's -- it's at 02:29:38:8 is where it starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise anybody in that -- in that picture?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That -- that house, that white house, is right on the main road. See those men kind of jammed into that balcony? Do you remember that sight when you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I want to go to another exhibit, 65 ter 3573. Sir, you've said that when you're there on the 13th travelling this area that you never -- well, did you see General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I've also answered that question that I didn't see a single senior officer from the staff in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could I get the ELMO? I see I don't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've also said that during this time that you were in Potocari you went through Bratunac as well, correct? Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: In order to reach Potocari one has to pass through Bratunac in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's why I asked the question. So you recall going to Bratunac twice, I guess, once on the way to Potocari and once on the way back.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you were all up and down that road between Konjevic Polje and Bratunac. Did you by chance stop by the Hotel Fontana --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I saw him nodding, but I didn't hear him say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you -- and you've testified during all of this time that you were there that you never saw Colonel Ljubisa Beara in Bratunac; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you go by the Hotel Fontana at any time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No. We only passed through Bratunac both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know that he had been at a room approved for him at the Hotel Fontana between 13 and 17 July according to this military document signed by -- or in the name of Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, just one moment. What's the objection, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is asked to speculate since this does not relate to his service or his department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's just being asked whether he knows or not, just as previously he didn't recognise some individuals from the photo that he was shown, he can answer this with a yes or a no. Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not believe that this is an appropriate question. By showing him these documents, one can put a question to the witness by asking if he was at the hotel --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've got to interrupt her at this point and I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau, you cannot replace or take our role in conducting the trial. That's for us to decide. If we notice that a question is not regular we usually stop, and if the objection is a valid one we usually grant it as well but not in this case. Let's proceed. Mr. Kerkez, can you answer the question, please? If you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't stop by to visit it, nor do I know where the hotel in Podrinje is. I was in Bratunac on perhaps two occasions only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I've got the original of this document that we acquired in Bratunac not -- not long ago and provided it to everyone, including the Beara Defence team a few days ago. Did they happen to show you this document to help refresh your recollection on whether or not Mr. Beara may have been in and around Bratunac and Potocari at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: Are you referring to this particular document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, the one on the screen.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you is there re-examination, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two questions only to clarify something about the consumption of fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkez, in answer to my learned friend the Prosecutor about the consumption of fuel, tell us this: In what way did you control the consumption of fuel if you were able to keep track of that at all?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO KERKEZ
utterances.text: I kept track of the consumption of fuel used only by the units that were under my professional supervision. As far as the consumption of fuel of the vehicles of the corps, this was the responsibility of the chief of the corps. That's why these organs existed. It was my duty to supervise and keep track of the department of the passenger vehicles and the Automobile Battalion that was under the control of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Kerkez, we have concluded your testimony. On behalf of the Trial Chamber I wish to thank you for having been kind enough to come over and give testimony. You're free to go. You will receive assistance from our staff. On behalf of everyone, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we go through, we've got -- our time is up, but I think we can stay a couple of more minutes to finish with the documents if you agree. Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Documents according to the 65 ter list 2D50 [as interpreted] and 2D549. These are the documents we used today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from anyone else? No objections. The documents are admitted. Any of the other Defence teams that cross-examined the witness? No documents. Mr. McCloskey. You used a few documents. Do you wish to tender any of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They're probably all already in, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think most of them are already in. Okay. I've got -- 65 ter 3178 was that Main Staff personnel employment record. I'm told that that was not in before. And then the -- the intercept of 12 July that we went over with him is 3574, and then the Bratunac Brigade document about the Hotel Fontana is 3573.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objections? Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have objections regarding the document 3573 on the ground of authenticity, because it is made on 25th of July, and it relates to the dates 13 to 17 July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is, of course, an issue which is why I brought out the original, and I would have asked my colleague to assist us in providing us the documents he received from the Hotel Fontana so that we may compare and determine to see if they found the same document. We went recently after our discussion on these documents, before filing any motion or anything, to see the same people they saw and we did. This was just a couple of weeks ago, and we got the materials that we got, including some of the things we saw that had Mr. Popovic's name on it. In addition to that, we found this original document, and we -- we intend to provide material regarding its authentication during the potential rebuttal stage if that need be on the alibi situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Because we do have the investigators that did that, how they found it, where they found it, the officer on the bottom of it who authorises this post facto approval was interviewed as well as the hotel people were interviewed, and that investigator and those people can be available really -- you know, it would be normal during the rebuttal stage if there's a challenge to it. But I would first ask the Court to ask Mr. Zivanovic to bring forward his documents so that we can compare the two. He's brought up the issue. He's called them into question. I think it is now incumbent upon him to come forward with the documents that hitherto he refused to provide us, and at a very minimum provide it to the Court, although I don't want -- you've got enough work. I think it's better that we the documents, we'll make the comparison, we'll sit down together. We've given them I think almost everything that we've got, though it's still in the process of that and I don't know if we have a hundred per cent of it or not, but the key ones we gave them as soon as it went through the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other objections? Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We also have an objection to make in relation to this document, because we've seen the original version of it only today and we haven't been given a chance to look at it before. All the more so, as we will have the opportunity in our further case to check the authenticity of some documents through our expert witnesses, we have not been given a chance to satisfy ourselves as to the authenticity of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They've had this document for several days. They could have seen it any time they wanted. Hearing this repeated refrain "that we did not have a chance to see pherograms or autopsy reports or -- it's -- I don't know what the purpose of those kind of comments are for, but of course they had a chance to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I need to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So this particular document will for the time can be marked for identification. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, can I add one point to this? I have interviewed the author of this document from the Bratunac Brigade recently just last week with Mr. Blasyck. He recognised his handwriting on it. That -- if that is not disclosed today it will be. The director of the Hotel Fontana and the parent company authenticated it. It's not an issue for this time for them to attack it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but it could become an issue. We are marking it for identification purposes only for the time being, and then later on if the question arises as to authenticity we'll decide. Yes, Mr. Nicholls -- Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One correction in the transcript. When I quoted the documents 2D500, it was entered as 2D50 only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Anything else? Nothing? I wish you all a nice weekend. We stand adjourned until Monday at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of July, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
